faq.question: Clexane vs Fraxiparine: when is each used, and why might one not be used?

sections.label: What they are
sections.text: Clexane is enoxaparin; Fraxiparine/Fraxaparin is nadroparin. Both are low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) anticoagulants. They overlap in purpose, but they are different medicines with product-specific dosing and must not be substituted dose-for-dose.

sections.label: When Clexane (enoxaparin) is used
sections.text: Current enoxaparin labeling includes prevention of DVT in selected surgical or acutely ill medical patients, treatment of acute DVT with or without pulmonary embolism, prevention of ischemic complications in unstable angina/non-Q-wave MI with aspirin, and treatment of acute STEMI with aspirin.

sections.label: When Fraxiparine (nadroparin) is used
sections.text: Current Fraxiparine product information includes prevention of thromboembolic disorders in surgical patients and high-risk medical/ICU patients, treatment of thromboembolic disorders, prevention of clotting during haemodialysis, and treatment of unstable angina/non-Q-wave MI.

sections.label: Why might Fraxiparine not be used?
sections.text: Renal function is an important reason. Nadroparin exposure increases as kidney function falls, increasing bleeding risk. Current Fraxiparine product information states that for treatment of thromboembolic disorders, unstable angina and non-Q-wave MI, nadroparin is contraindicated in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min). Its prophylaxis recommendations are different and include dose reduction in severe renal impairment, so 'renal failure means never use Fraxiparine' would be too broad.

sections.label: Why might Clexane be used instead?
sections.text: Enoxaparin also accumulates in renal impairment and bleeding risk increases, but current prescribing information provides specific reduced prophylactic and treatment regimens when CrCl is <30 mL/min. Therefore severe renal impairment does not automatically exclude enoxaparin under its product labeling; the dose/indication must be adjusted and verified.

sections.label: What does NOT decide between them?
sections.text: Do not choose based on serum creatinine alone, trade-name familiarity, or an assumed dose conversion. Check estimated renal function (especially CrCl), the indication, bleeding risk, platelet history/count, the exact ordered product, and the applicable local protocol/order.

sections.label: CCU nursing takeaway
sections.text: For ACS or another anticoagulation indication, first identify exactly which LMWH is ordered and why. Before administration, check bleeding risk, platelets and renal function. If renal function is severely impaired, stop and verify the product-specific order/protocol rather than automatically giving the usual dose or swapping Clexane and Fraxiparine.

faq.verification: Current drug-specific renal and indication statements verified 25 Sep 2026 against current DailyMed enoxaparin prescribing information and current Fraxiparine product information. Gaza-specific preference/selection between enoxaparin and nadroparin remains unverified; do not infer that one is routinely preferred locally.

faq.question: What is heart failure?

sections.label: Core idea
sections.text: Heart failure means the heart is not functioning well enough to meet the body's needs without abnormal filling pressures. At the bedside, think in two directions: congestion and poor perfusion.

sections.label: Congestion
sections.text: Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, leg edema, raised JVP and fluid/weight gain.

sections.label: Poor perfusion
sections.text: Hypotension, cold/clammy skin, weak pulse, confusion and low urine output.

sections.label: Left vs right
sections.text: Left-sided HF mainly backs up into the lungs → dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles and pulmonary edema. Right-sided HF mainly backs up into the systemic veins → peripheral edema, raised JVP and abdominal/hepatic congestion.

sections.label: EF
sections.text: Ejection fraction is the percentage of blood in the LV ejected with each contraction. Current 2026 ESC guidance uses an updated LVEF-based classification; do not judge a patient's clinical severity from EF alone.

sections.label: Nursing focus
sections.text: Breathing + BP + rhythm + perfusion + urine output + fluid balance. Escalate sudden severe dyspnea, pulmonary edema, falling BP, altered consciousness, dangerous arrhythmia, very low urine output or ischemic chest pain.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: HF patients may be 'wet' from congestion, 'cold' from poor perfusion, or both.

faq.verification: Heart-failure framework reviewed against current 2026 ESC heart-failure guidance.

faq.question: What is DCM?

sections.label: Meaning
sections.text: DCM = dilated cardiomyopathy. The ventricles, especially the LV, become enlarged and contract weakly, so cardiac output can fall.

sections.label: What you may see
sections.text: It often presents with heart-failure features such as dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, edema and crackles if congested. Arrhythmias may also occur.

sections.label: Why it matters in CCU
sections.text: A patient with DCM can deteriorate with acute heart failure, arrhythmia, low cardiac output or cardiogenic shock.

sections.label: Nursing focus
sections.text: Monitor BP, rhythm, SpO₂, breathing, edema, urine output and perfusion.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: DCM = dilated heart + weak pump → heart-failure and arrhythmia risk.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic quick clinical reference.

faq.question: What can dilated cardiomyopathy result from?

sections.label: High-yield causes
sections.text: Genetic/familial disease; myocarditis; alcohol or cardiotoxic drugs; ischemic heart disease or previous MI; peripartum cardiomyopathy; long-standing tachyarrhythmias; and some endocrine, metabolic or nutritional disorders. Sometimes no clear cause is found.

sections.label: Simple idea
sections.text: Many different conditions can damage or weaken the myocardium enough to produce ventricular dilation and poor contraction.

sections.label: CCU priority
sections.text: At the bedside, also ask whether the DCM patient is currently in heart failure, an arrhythmia or a low-output state.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic quick clinical reference.

faq.question: What is the difference between ischemic heart disease (IHD) and myocardial infarction (MI)?

sections.label: IHD
sections.text: Ischemic heart disease is the broader disease state caused by inadequate coronary blood supply. It can include stable angina, unstable angina, MI and chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy.

sections.label: MI
sections.text: Myocardial infarction is a specific event in which myocardial ischemia is severe/prolonged enough to cause myocardial injury with necrosis in the appropriate ischemic clinical context.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: MI is one possible manifestation of ischemic heart disease, but a patient can have IHD without currently having an MI. Example: stable exertional angina.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic quick clinical reference.

faq.question: What does CK-MB mean, and how is it different from total CK?

sections.label: Meaning
sections.text: CK = creatine kinase. CK-MB is the MB isoenzyme of creatine kinase. CK isoenzymes are built from M and B subunits: M = muscle subunit, B = brain subunit.

sections.label: Difference
sections.text: Total CK is nonspecific and can rise with skeletal-muscle injury. CK-MB is more cardiac-associated than total CK, but it is an older and less specific cardiac biomarker than modern troponin testing.

sections.label: CCU takeaway
sections.text: Interpret CK/CK-MB together with symptoms, ECG and the overall ischemic clinical picture; biomarker elevation alone does not define MI.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic clarification; local use of CK/CK-MB reflects reported current CCU practice, not a universal standard.

faq.question: What is cardioversion, and how is it different from defibrillation?

sections.label: Cardioversion
sections.text: Synchronized cardioversion is an electrical shock timed to the R wave. It is typically used for an unstable tachyarrhythmia when a pulse is present.

sections.label: Defibrillation
sections.text: Defibrillation is an unsynchronized shock used for cardiac arrest with VF or pulseless VT.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Cardioversion = synchronized + pulse. Defibrillation = unsynchronized + VF/pulseless VT arrest.

faq.verification: Reviewed against current 2025 AHA adult advanced-life-support guidance.

faq.question: Which cardiac-arrest rhythms are shockable? Is pulseless VT really shockable?

sections.label: Shockable
sections.text: Yes. Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT) are the two shockable cardiac-arrest rhythms.

sections.label: Non-shockable
sections.text: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole are non-shockable.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: VF + pVT = shock. PEA + asystole = no shock.

faq.verification: Reviewed against current 2025 AHA cardiac-arrest guidance.

faq.question: What is pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?

sections.label: Meaning
sections.text: PEA means organized electrical activity is visible on the monitor/ECG but the patient has no palpable pulse and no effective circulation.

sections.label: Important point
sections.text: PEA does not have one specific ECG appearance. The defining feature is electrical activity without a pulse.

sections.label: Action concept
sections.text: It is a non-shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm: start/continue high-quality CPR, follow the arrest algorithm and search for reversible causes.

faq.verification: Reviewed against current 2025 AHA adult cardiac-arrest guidance.

faq.question: What is the difference between an ECG electrode and a lead?

sections.label: Electrode
sections.text: The physical sticker/wire touching the patient's skin.

sections.label: Lead
sections.text: The electrical view calculated from the electrodes.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Electrodes touch the patient. Leads are what the machine sees. A standard 12-lead ECG uses 10 electrodes to produce 12 views.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic ECG clarification.

faq.question: What is the difference between 3-lead monitoring and a 12-lead ECG?

sections.label: 3-lead monitoring
sections.text: Usually three electrodes are used for continuous bedside heart-rate and rhythm monitoring.

sections.label: 12-lead ECG
sections.text: Uses 10 electrodes to generate 12 electrical views and gives much more diagnostic information, especially for ischemia and conduction abnormalities.

sections.label: Practical takeaway
sections.text: Telemetry tells you what the rhythm is doing continuously; a 12-lead gives a fuller diagnostic snapshot.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic telemetry clarification.

faq.question: What is the pleth waveform on the bedside monitor?

sections.label: Meaning
sections.text: The pleth waveform comes from the pulse-oximeter probe and represents pulsatile changes in blood volume/perfusion at the probe site.

sections.label: What it gives
sections.text: It supports SpO₂ measurement and pulse rate (PR). It is different from the ECG waveform, which reflects cardiac electrical activity.

sections.label: Practical point
sections.text: Depending on monitor layout, ECG and pleth waveforms may both be displayed at the same time.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic bedside-monitor clarification.

faq.question: How is ECG monitoring handled during CPR?

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Defibrillator pads can both monitor the rhythm and deliver shocks. They are the key electrical interface during a code.

sections.label: Artifact
sections.text: Chest compressions create major ECG artifact, so rhythm analysis is done during brief pauses while interruptions in compressions are minimized.

sections.label: Electrodes
sections.text: Existing ECG electrodes can remain if they do not interfere, but defibrillator pads are the priority during cardiac arrest.

faq.verification: Reviewed against current AHA resuscitation principles.

faq.question: How do I differentiate cardiogenic shock from hypovolemic and other shock types?

sections.label: Memory model
sections.text: Ask: is the tank empty, the pump failing, the pipes too wide, or flow obstructed?

sections.label: Cardiogenic
sections.text: Pump failure. Often hypotension + cold/clammy skin + weak pulse; lungs may be wet/crackly and JVP may be raised.

sections.label: Hypovolemic
sections.text: Empty tank. Often hypotension + tachycardia + cold/clammy skin, flat neck veins, clear lungs, and a history of bleeding or fluid loss.

sections.label: Distributive
sections.text: Vessels are too dilated. In septic shock the patient may be warm with bounding pulses early.

sections.label: Obstructive
sections.text: Blood flow is physically blocked, such as with tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism.

sections.label: Important rule
sections.text: Do not diagnose the shock type from one sign alone. Combine history, BP, pulse, lungs, JVP, urine output and mental status.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic shock-differentiation clarification.

faq.question: How can I easily understand norepinephrine vs dobutamine?

sections.label: Norepinephrine
sections.text: Think PRESSURE. It mainly increases vascular tone and is used when blood pressure/perfusion is too low.

sections.label: Dobutamine
sections.text: Think PUMP. It mainly increases cardiac contractility and is used when the heart is pumping too weakly.

sections.label: Why both may appear
sections.text: A patient can have both a weak pump and dangerously low pressure, so both drugs may be used for different hemodynamic goals.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Norepinephrine = pressure. Dobutamine = pump.

faq.verification: Core Nursing Diagnostic simplified CCU explanation; dosing/administration remains product/order/protocol specific.

faq.question: Can a patient have an MI without obvious ECG changes, and how do we know where the MI is?

sections.label: Yes
sections.text: A myocardial infarction can occur without diagnostic ST-elevation or other obvious changes on the first ECG. NSTEMI may show ST depression or T-wave inversion, but the ECG can also be nondiagnostic.

sections.label: What makes it an MI
sections.text: Acute MI requires a rise and/or fall in cardiac troponin with at least one value above the assay's 99th-percentile upper reference limit, plus evidence of acute myocardial ischemia such as ischemic symptoms, ischemic ECG changes, new pathologic Q waves, ischemic imaging findings, or coronary thrombus.

sections.label: If the ECG does not localize it
sections.text: Troponin confirms myocardial injury but does not tell you the wall. Location may be identified by echocardiographic regional wall-motion abnormalities, coronary angiography, or other cardiac imaging. Extra leads may help when a standard 12-lead misses posterior or right-ventricular involvement.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Normal ECG does not rule out MI. Troponin + ischemic evidence diagnoses MI; echo/angiography can help localize it.

faq.verification: Reviewed 30 Sep 2026 against the Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction and current 2025 ACC/AHA acute coronary syndrome guidance.

faq.question: What does ACS mean, and why is it called Acute Coronary Syndrome?

sections.label: Meaning
sections.text: ACS = Acute Coronary Syndrome: a group of acute conditions caused by a sudden reduction or interruption of coronary blood flow to the myocardium.

sections.label: Why this name
sections.text: Acute = sudden/new. Coronary = involves the coronary arteries/blood flow. Syndrome = an umbrella of related clinical conditions rather than one single diagnosis.

sections.label: What it includes
sections.text: ACS includes unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: ACS = sudden coronary blood-flow problem causing acute myocardial ischemia.

faq.verification: Reviewed 30 Sep 2026 against current 2025 ACC/AHA acute coronary syndrome guidance.

faq.question: What is the clear diagnostic difference between unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI?

sections.label: Unstable angina (UA)
sections.text: Acute myocardial ischemia without evidence of acute myocardial infarction. Troponin does not show the dynamic MI-level rise/fall pattern. The ECG may be normal or may show transient ischemic changes such as ST depression or T-wave inversion.

sections.label: NSTEMI
sections.text: Acute MI criteria are met: cardiac troponin shows a rise/fall with at least one value above the assay's 99th-percentile upper reference limit, plus evidence of acute myocardial ischemia. There is no qualifying persistent STEMI-pattern ST elevation; the ECG may show ST depression, T-wave inversion, or be nondiagnostic.

sections.label: STEMI
sections.text: The patient has an acute ischemic presentation with a qualifying STEMI-pattern ECG. This triggers urgent reperfusion assessment; do not wait for troponin confirmation before activating the STEMI pathway when ECG criteria and clinical context fit.

sections.label: Fast comparison
sections.text: UA = ischemia without infarction. NSTEMI = infarction without a STEMI ECG pattern. STEMI = infarction with a STEMI ECG pattern.

sections.label: Important trap
sections.text: Troponin elevation alone means myocardial injury, not automatically MI. MI also requires evidence that the injury is due to acute ischemia.

faq.verification: Reviewed 30 Sep 2026 against current ACS guidance and the current universal-definition framework for myocardial infarction.

faq.question: Is there chronic coronary disease, and how is it different from ACS?

sections.label: Chronic coronary disease
sections.text: Yes. Chronic coronary disease (CCD) is the long-term coronary disease state and includes obstructive or nonobstructive CAD, chronic angina syndromes, and patients with prior MI or coronary revascularization after acute issues have stabilized.

sections.label: ACS
sections.text: ACS is an acute event or syndrome caused by a sudden reduction in coronary blood flow, including unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI.

sections.label: Relationship
sections.text: A patient with chronic coronary disease can later develop an ACS. After an ACS stabilizes, the patient may again be managed as chronic coronary disease.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: CCD = long-term coronary disease. ACS = something acute happened now.

faq.verification: Reviewed 30 Sep 2026 against the 2023 AHA/ACC Chronic Coronary Disease guideline and current 2025 ACS guidance.

faq.question: Why do some CCU interviewers say MI can be very severe in young patients because of collateral circulation?

sections.label: Interview concept
sections.text: If severe coronary narrowing develops slowly over time, collateral coronary arteries may enlarge and provide alternative blood flow. A younger patient with a sudden occlusion may not have had a long period of severe stenosis to develop robust collaterals, so the ischemic territory can be large.

sections.label: Important correction
sections.text: Do not say that young MI patients generally have higher mortality than older MI patients. Overall, older age is associated with higher MI mortality. The collateral explanation describes one possible mechanism for why an individual young MI can be abrupt and severe.

sections.label: Correct terminology
sections.text: Say coronary collateral arteries or collateral circulation, not collateral veins.

sections.label: Interview answer
sections.text: A young patient may have less-developed collateral circulation if there was no long-standing severe coronary stenosis, so a sudden major occlusion may have less alternative blood supply to the myocardium.

faq.verification: Reviewed 30 Sep 2026 against contemporary coronary-collateral literature, including a 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis; preserves the locally reported interview framing while correcting the mortality claim.

faq.question: At what age do coronary collateral arteries stop growing?

sections.label: No fixed age
sections.text: There is no specific age at which coronary collateral arteries stop growing or enlarging.

sections.label: What drives development
sections.text: Collateral enlargement is driven mainly by the presence and duration of severe coronary stenosis/ischemia, pressure-flow gradients, and individual biology rather than by reaching a particular age.

sections.label: Age effect
sections.text: Older age does not automatically mean better collateral circulation. Aging may actually impair collateral growth/function, so age alone is not a reliable predictor.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Think chronic stenosis and ischemic stimulus, not an age cutoff.

faq.verification: Reviewed 30 Sep 2026 against contemporary coronary-collateral literature; no fixed age cutoff is established.

faq.question: What about other cardiac enzymes/biomarkers besides troponin in suspected MI?

sections.label: Troponin
sections.text: Cardiac troponin I or T is the preferred biomarker for acute myocardial injury. A dynamic rise/fall is central to diagnosing acute MI when combined with evidence of acute myocardial ischemia.

sections.label: CK-MB
sections.text: CK-MB is an older and less sensitive/specific marker. When cardiac troponin is available, CK-MB usually adds little diagnostic value. If troponin is unavailable, serial CK-MB may still support the diagnosis together with symptoms and ECG.

sections.label: Other older markers
sections.text: Myoglobin rises early but is very nonspecific. Total CK can rise with skeletal-muscle injury. LDH and AST are historical MI markers and are not routinely used for modern MI diagnosis.

sections.label: Key nursing point
sections.text: Biomarkers indicate myocardial injury; they do not decide STEMI versus NSTEMI. The ECG and clinical presentation determine the STEMI pathway, and reperfusion assessment should not be delayed while waiting for biomarkers when STEMI criteria are present.

sections.label: Terminology
sections.text: 'Cardiac enzymes' is a common older phrase. Troponin itself is a cardiac biomarker/protein, not an enzyme.

faq.verification: Reviewed 30 Sep 2026 against current ACS/MI diagnostic standards. Local CCU use of CK/CK-MB may reflect resource availability.

faq.question: Why is IV amiodarone commonly diluted in D5W rather than normal saline?

sections.label: Main reason
sections.text: For common IV amiodarone concentrate formulations, manufacturer preparation and stability data specify D5W. The reason is formulation compatibility/stability—not because the patient needs glucose.

sections.label: Practical nursing rule
sections.text: Prepare and dilute IV amiodarone according to the exact product label, written order and local protocol. Do not automatically substitute normal saline for D5W.

sections.label: Important nuance
sections.text: Do not memorize 'normal saline always causes precipitation.' Compatibility can depend on the exact formulation, concentration, container and conditions. The safest rule is to use the diluent validated for the product in hand.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Amiodarone infusion → think D5W for compatibility/stability; verify the exact product before preparation.

faq.verification: Verified 30 Sep 2026 against current DailyMed IV amiodarone labeling, which documents physical compatibility/stability in D5W. Product-specific labeling remains controlling.

medications.name: LOSARTAN
medications.availability: Palestinian-system evidence: the Palestinian Essential Medicines List includes losartan 50 mg tablet as an antihypertensive. Current stock/availability at a specific Gaza facility has not been independently confirmed.
medications.use: Main use: treatment of hypertension. Current labeling also includes selected hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy and diabetic nephropathy in type 2 diabetes.
medications.administration: Oral tablet. The Palestinian Essential Medicines List identifies a 50 mg tablet. Administer only according to the prescribed order; verify the product/strength in hand and current local protocol.
medications.monitor: • Check blood pressure and watch for symptomatic hypotension, especially with volume or salt depletion. • Review renal function because renal deterioration can occur in susceptible patients. • Monitor serum potassium because hyperkalemia can occur. • Review concurrent potassium-raising drugs, NSAIDs, lithium, and other renin-angiotensin system blockers. • Pregnancy is a major safety issue: current labeling carries a fetal-toxicity boxed warning.
medications.why: Blocking angiotensin II AT1-receptor effects reduces vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated effects, lowering blood pressure. Renal function and potassium matter because the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system also helps regulate renal perfusion and potassium balance.
medications.source: Verified update · Palestinian EML + current DailyMed
medications.memoryUse: ARB used mainly to lower blood pressure in hypertension.
medications.memoryDanger: Watch K+, renal function and hypotension. Major red flag: pregnancy.
medications.mechanism: Selectively blocks angiotensin II binding to the AT1 receptor, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone effects.
medications.mechanismBasis: Verified against current losartan prescribing information; Palestinian relevance supported by the Palestinian Essential Medicines List. Gaza facility-specific stock remains unconfirmed.

lessons.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: ACS = acute myocardial ischemia from reduced coronary blood flow. It includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI.

sections.label: Differentiate
sections.text:
• Unstable angina: ischemia without biomarker evidence of myocardial necrosis.
• NSTEMI: myocardial infarction without persistent ST elevation; ECG may show ST depression/T-wave changes.
• STEMI: acute ischemic presentation with compatible ST elevation.

sections.label: Recognize
sections.text:
• Chest pressure/tightness/heaviness
• Radiation to arm, shoulder, jaw, neck, or back
• Dyspnea
• Sweating
• Nausea/vomiting
• Dizziness

sections.label: First nursing actions
sections.text:
• ABC assessment and vital signs
• Cardiac monitoring/rhythm check
• Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly
• Establish IV access
• Escalate immediately for ischemic ECG changes, hypotension, serious arrhythmia, worsening dyspnea, altered consciousness, or deterioration
• Obtain ordered blood tests and give prescribed ACS treatment
• Oxygen only when indicated by oxygenation/clinical status and local protocol

sections.label: Key rule
sections.text: Do not wait for a biomarker result before escalating a patient with concerning ischemic symptoms, ECG changes, or hemodynamic instability.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson. ACS concepts taught using current ACC/AHA ACS guidance.

lessons.title: Complete Heart Block (CHB)

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: Complete heart block = third-degree AV block. Atrial impulses do not conduct to the ventricles, so atria and ventricles beat independently.

sections.label: ECG hallmark
sections.text: P waves and QRS complexes march separately with no fixed PR relationship. This is AV dissociation.

sections.label: Why it is dangerous
sections.text: A slow ventricular escape rhythm can reduce cardiac output and cause dizziness, syncope, hypotension, confusion, ischemia, acute heart failure, shock, or cardiac arrest.

sections.label: Differentiate from sinus bradycardia
sections.text: Sinus bradycardia: each P wave conducts to a QRS. CHB: P waves and QRS complexes are independent.

sections.label: First nursing actions
sections.text:
• Look at the patient first
• ABC assessment
• Check pulse, BP, consciousness, SpO₂, and symptoms
• Continuous monitoring and 12-lead ECG
• Establish IV access
• Escalate rapidly if symptomatic or unstable
• Prepare for pacing if required

sections.label: Common causes
sections.text:
• MI/ischemia
• Beta-blockers
• Calcium-channel blockers
• Digoxin
• Hypoxia
• Hyperkalemia

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: CHB = atria and ventricles beat independently. If perfusion is poor, escalate and prepare for pacing.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson; bradycardia instability concepts aligned with current AHA guidance.

sections.label: 10 electrodes, 12 leads
sections.text: A 12-lead ECG uses 10 physical electrodes: 4 limb electrodes + 6 chest electrodes. The machine derives 12 electrical views.

sections.label: Electrode vs lead
sections.text: Electrode = the physical sticker/wire touching the patient. Lead = the electrical view the machine sees.

sections.label: Chest electrode placement
sections.text:
• V1: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border
• V2: 4th intercostal space, left sternal border
• V3: halfway between V2 and V4
• V4: 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line
• V5: same horizontal level as V4, anterior axillary line
• V6: same horizontal level as V4, midaxillary line

sections.label: Waves
sections.text: P wave = atrial depolarization. QRS = ventricular depolarization. T wave = ventricular repolarization.

sections.label: Limb colors used locally
sections.text: IEC system commonly seen locally: RA/R = red, LA/L = yellow, LL/F = green, RL/N = black. F = Foot; N = Neutral.

sections.label: Common mistake
sections.text: Placing V1 and V2 too high can create a misleading tracing.

sections.label: What telemetry is
sections.text: Telemetry/bedside ECG monitoring continuously displays cardiac electrical rhythm. It is not the same as a diagnostic 12-lead ECG.

sections.label: 3-lead monitoring
sections.text: A common setup uses three electrodes for continuous heart rate and rhythm monitoring.

sections.label: ECG waveform vs pleth
sections.text: ECG waveform comes from ECG electrodes and reflects electrical activity. Pleth waveform comes from the pulse-oximeter probe and reflects pulsatile blood flow; it gives SpO₂ and pulse rate.

sections.label: Read a rhythm in order
sections.text: Patient → Rate → Regularity → P waves → PR interval → QRS → P/QRS relationship.

sections.label: Useful basics
sections.text:
• 6-second strip: QRS count × 10 ≈ heart rate
• Regular rhythm: 300 ÷ large boxes between R waves
• PR normally about 0.12–0.20 sec
• QRS normally <0.12 sec

sections.label: Artifact rule
sections.text: If the monitor looks chaotic but the patient is awake, talking, and has a strong regular pulse, suspect artifact. Check the patient and pulse before treating the monitor.

lessons.title: Dangerous Rhythms

sections.label: First principle
sections.text: Patient + pulse + rhythm. In suspected arrest, if no definite pulse is found promptly, begin the arrest response.

sections.label: Shockable arrest rhythms
sections.text:
• Ventricular fibrillation (VF)
• Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT)

sections.label: Non-shockable arrest rhythms
sections.text:
• Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)
• Asystole

sections.label: VT rule
sections.text: Always ask: does the patient have a pulse? Pulseless VT follows the cardiac-arrest pathway. VT with a pulse follows the stable/unstable tachyarrhythmia pathway.

sections.label: PEA
sections.text: PEA means organized electrical activity is seen but there is no pulse. It has no single ECG appearance.

sections.label: Instability signs
sections.text:
• Hypotension
• Acute altered mental status
• Signs of shock
• Ischemic chest discomfort
• Acute heart failure

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: VF + pVT = shockable. PEA + asystole = non-shockable.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson; arrest rhythm classification aligned with current AHA guidance.

lessons.title: Defibrillation vs Cardioversion vs Pacing

sections.label: Start with two questions
sections.text: Does the patient have a pulse? If yes, are they stable or unstable?

sections.label: Defibrillation
sections.text: Unsynchronized shock used for cardiac arrest with VF or pulseless VT. PEA and asystole are not shockable.

sections.label: Synchronized cardioversion
sections.text: A timed shock synchronized to the R wave, typically used for an unstable tachyarrhythmia when a pulse is present.

sections.label: Why synchronization matters
sections.text: Synchronization avoids delivering the shock during the vulnerable T-wave period.

sections.label: Important exception
sections.text: Polymorphic VT requiring shock is treated with an unsynchronized shock because reliable synchronization is not possible.

sections.label: Pacing
sections.text: Repeated electrical stimulation used for dangerous symptomatic bradycardia/high-grade block such as CHB.

sections.label: Capture
sections.text: Electrical capture = pacing spike followed by a QRS. Mechanical capture = a corresponding pulse/BP/perfusion response. Confirm both.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Defib = VF/pVT arrest. Cardioversion = unstable fast rhythm with pulse. Pacing = dangerous bradycardia.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson; concepts aligned with current AHA guidance.

lessons.title: Sudden Deterioration in CCU: What Do You Do First?

sections.label: Core sequence
sections.text: Patient first → ABC → monitor → identify danger → escalate → reassess.

sections.label: First 30–60 seconds
sections.text:
• A Airway: can the patient talk? Any obstruction?
• B Breathing: RR, effort, SpO₂, breath sounds
• C Circulation: pulse, BP, rhythm, skin/perfusion
• D Disability: consciousness/confusion
• E Exposure: bleeding, edema, lines, obvious cause

sections.label: Red flags
sections.text:
• New severe chest pain
• Sudden dyspnea
• Falling SpO₂
• Hypotension or a marked BP fall
• New confusion/reduced consciousness
• Very fast or very slow heart rate with symptoms
• Dangerous arrhythmia
• Cold/clammy skin or weak pulse
• No pulse
• Sudden major bleeding

sections.label: Practical actions
sections.text:
• ECG + BP + SpO₂ monitoring
• Ensure IV access
• Position appropriately
• Give oxygen when indicated
• Obtain 12-lead ECG when relevant
• Prepare emergency equipment/medications as directed
• Reassess after every intervention

sections.label: Examples
sections.text: Monitor shows VT → look at patient and check pulse. Worsening chest pain → vitals + rhythm + 12-lead + escalate; do not wait for biomarkers. Unresponsive patient → check responsiveness, breathing and pulse; if pulseless, start the arrest response.

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: Cardiogenic shock = the heart cannot pump enough blood to perfuse the organs. Think: weak pump → low cardiac output → organ hypoperfusion.

sections.label: Suspect it when
sections.text:
• Hypotension
• Cold/clammy extremities
• Weak peripheral pulses
• Confusion/reduced consciousness
• Low urine output
• Tachycardia or significant bradycardia
• Dyspnea/crackles may coexist

sections.label: Common CCU causes
sections.text:
• Acute MI
• Severe heart failure
• Serious arrhythmia
• Mechanical complication after MI
• Severe valve dysfunction

sections.label: First nursing response
sections.text: ABC → BP → rhythm → perfusion → escalate. Assess SpO₂/breathing, consciousness, skin, pulses, urine output, and ensure monitoring/IV access.

sections.label: Important mistake
sections.text: Do not automatically give a large IV fluid bolus. If the pump is failing, excess fluid can worsen pulmonary edema.

sections.label: Cardiogenic vs hypovolemic
sections.text: Cardiogenic: pump failure; often cold/clammy, weak pulse, possible crackles/pulmonary edema, JVP may be raised. Hypovolemic: empty tank; often cold/clammy, tachycardic, flat neck veins, clear lungs, with bleeding/dehydration/fluid-loss history.

sections.label: Other shock patterns
sections.text: Distributive shock: vessels are too dilated; septic shock may be warm early. Obstructive shock: flow is blocked, e.g. tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Cardiogenic = weak pump, often wet lungs/full veins. Hypovolemic = empty tank, usually clear lungs/flat veins. Use the whole clinical picture, not one sign.

lessons.title: Norepinephrine vs Dobutamine

sections.label: The easiest way to remember
sections.text: Norepinephrine = Pressure. Dobutamine = Pump.

sections.label: Norepinephrine
sections.text: Think: the blood pressure/perfusion is too low. Norepinephrine mainly increases vascular tone and raises blood pressure.

sections.label: Dobutamine
sections.text: Think: the heart itself is pumping too weakly. Dobutamine mainly increases cardiac contractility and cardiac output.

sections.label: Why both may be used
sections.text: If a patient has both a weak pump and dangerously low pressure, the team may use dobutamine for pump support and norepinephrine for pressure support.

sections.label: What you monitor
sections.text: Norepinephrine: BP/MAP, rhythm, perfusion, urine output, IV site. Dobutamine: HR/rhythm, BP, perfusion, urine output.

sections.label: Safety memory
sections.text: These are titrated IV infusions. Do not memorize one universal mL/hour rate; the rate depends on the ordered dose and prepared concentration.

sections.label: Potassium K⁺
sections.text: Potassium strongly affects cardiac electrical activity. Low K⁺ can cause ectopy/arrhythmias and may show flat T waves or U waves. High K⁺ may show tall peaked T waves and, when severe, widening QRS/bradyarrhythmia/arrest.

sections.label: Magnesium Mg²⁺
sections.text: Low Mg²⁺ makes the heart electrically irritable and can contribute to ventricular arrhythmias. It can also make hypokalemia harder to correct. Magnesium is especially important in torsades de pointes.

sections.label: Calcium Ca²⁺
sections.text: Calcium affects contraction and the QT interval. Low Ca²⁺ tends to prolong QT; high Ca²⁺ tends to shorten QT.

sections.label: Practical CCU example
sections.text: A patient on a loop diuretic develops frequent PVCs. Do not only think 'the rhythm changed'—also check K⁺ and Mg²⁺.

sections.label: Nursing safety
sections.text: If an electrolyte abnormality is accompanied by rhythm/ECG changes, monitor continuously and escalate promptly. Never give IV potassium as a rapid IV push.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: K⁺ = rhythm priority. Mg²⁺ = rhythm stability. Ca²⁺ = contraction + QT.

lessons.title: Furosemide in the CCU

sections.label: Why the patient may receive it
sections.text: Think fluid overload/congestion, especially in heart failure: breathlessness + crackles + edema.

sections.label: What furosemide does
sections.text: Furosemide is a loop diuretic. More urine → less excess fluid → less congestion.

sections.label: What improvement may look like
sections.text:
• Easier breathing
• Less edema
• Fewer crackles
• Reduced fluid overload

sections.label: What the nurse monitors
sections.text:
• BP
• Urine output
• Potassium K⁺
• Renal function
• Overall fluid status

sections.label: Main problems to watch for
sections.text:
• Hypotension
• Excessive volume depletion/dehydration
• Hypokalemia
• Worsening renal function

sections.label: CCU connection
sections.text: If a patient receiving furosemide develops new PVCs or another rhythm change, think about K⁺ and Mg²⁺ as possible contributors.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Furosemide = remove excess fluid. Watch BP, urine output, kidney function and K⁺.

lessons.title: Heart Failure — Practical CCU View

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump enough blood effectively or requires abnormally high filling pressures. Clinically, think in two directions: congestion and poor perfusion.

sections.label: Congestion
sections.text: Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, leg edema, raised JVP, and fluid/weight gain.

sections.label: Poor perfusion
sections.text: Hypotension, cold/clammy skin, weak pulse, confusion, and low urine output.

sections.label: Left vs right
sections.text: Left-sided HF mainly backs up into the lungs → dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, pulmonary edema. Right-sided HF mainly backs up into the systemic veins → peripheral edema, raised JVP, abdominal/hepatic congestion.

sections.label: EF
sections.text: Ejection fraction is the percentage of LV blood ejected with each contraction. HFrEF = reduced EF. HFpEF = preserved EF but impaired filling/stiffness. Do not judge severity from EF alone.

sections.label: Nursing focus
sections.text: Breathing + BP + rhythm + perfusion + urine output + fluid balance. Escalate sudden severe dyspnea, pulmonary edema, falling BP, altered consciousness, dangerous arrhythmia, very low urine output, or ischemic chest pain.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: HF patients may be 'wet' from congestion, 'cold' from poor perfusion, or both.

lessons.sourceNote: Quick clinical reference from this Core Nursing Diagnostic session.

lessons.title: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)

sections.label: What it means
sections.text: DCM = dilated cardiomyopathy. The ventricles, especially the LV, become enlarged and contract weakly → cardiac output falls.

sections.label: What it causes
sections.text: Often presents as heart failure: dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, edema, crackles if congested, and arrhythmias. Severe cases can develop low-output states or cardiogenic shock.

sections.label: Common causes
sections.text:
• Genetic/familial disease
• Myocarditis
• Alcohol or cardiotoxic drugs
• Ischemic heart disease/previous MI
• Peripartum cardiomyopathy
• Long-standing tachyarrhythmias
• Some endocrine, metabolic, or nutritional disorders
• Sometimes no clear cause is found

sections.label: Nursing focus
sections.text: Monitor BP, rhythm, SpO₂, breathing, edema, urine output, and perfusion.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: DCM = dilated heart + weak pump → heart failure risk.

lessons.sourceNote: Quick clinical reference from this Core Nursing Diagnostic session.

lessons.title: Ischemic Heart Disease vs Myocardial Infarction

sections.label: IHD
sections.text: Ischemic heart disease is the broader disease state caused by reduced coronary blood supply. It can present as stable angina, unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, or chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy.

sections.label: MI
sections.text: Myocardial infarction is a specific event in which ischemia is severe/prolonged enough to cause myocardial cell death.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: All MI is ischemic heart disease, but not all ischemic heart disease is MI. A patient with stable exertional angina has IHD but is not necessarily having an MI.
